title: Gender And Sexuality
sources_used: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Expand LGBTQIA+. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• 18(a). Explain the effects of the gender-based wage gap on women and their families.
  • The gender wage gap is the difference between women’s and men’s earnings. It reflects
  • factors including occupational segregation, unequal care responsibilities, differences in
  • working hours and discrimination. It is broader than unequal pay for identical work.
  • Reduced economic independence: Lower earnings can increase women’s dependence on
  • partners or relatives and reduce their ability to make independent decisions.
  • Lower household resources: Families have less income available for food, housing,
  • healthcare and education. This is particularly serious in households dependent on women’s
  • earnings.
  • Reduced bargaining power: Lower earnings may weaken women’s influence over household
  • spending, residence and employment decisions.
  • Cumulative disadvantage: Reduced earnings limit savings, property ownership, retirement
  • contributions and financial security in later life.
  • Reinforcement of unequal care roles: When women earn less, families may decide that
  • women should reduce paid work to provide care. This can further reduce their experience
  • and future earnings.
  • Effects on children: Financial insecurity can restrict children’s opportunities. Persistent wage
  • inequality may also reinforce expectations that men’s work is more valuable.
  • Example: A family may ask the lower-paid mother to leave employment when childcare
  • becomes expensive, deepening her long-term disadvantage.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; explained effects — 4; example/conclusion — 1.
  • 18(b). Explain the relevance of liberal feminist principles for improving women’s access to
  • education.
  • Liberal feminism emphasises equal rights, individual freedom and equal opportunities. It
  • argues that gender should not determine access to education or the ability to develop one’s
  • talents.
  • Equal admission opportunities: Girls and women should have fair access to schools,
  • colleges, training and all fields of study.
  • Removal of discriminatory rules: Institutions should eliminate practices that restrict
  • subjects, activities or leadership roles according to gender.
  • Material support: Scholarships, affordable education, transport and accommodation can
  • help remove practical barriers to participation.
  • Freedom of choice: Women should be able to choose subjects and careers according to their
  • interests rather than gender expectations.
  • Gender-sensitive teaching: Textbooks, classroom interactions and career guidance should
  • challenge assumptions that particular abilities belong to one gender.
  • Institutional reform: Accessible grievance procedures, protection against harassment and
  • support for students with caregiving responsibilities can improve retention.
  • Example: Supporting women’s participation in engineering through fair admissions, financial
  • assistance and mentoring puts liberal feminist principles into practice.
  • Liberal feminism provides a strong basis for educational reform, although formal equality
  • alone may not overcome deeper caste, class and gender inequalities.
  • Suggested marking: Principles — 2; educational applications — 3; example/assessment — 1.
  • 19(a). Explain dowry violence with reference to harassment connected with marriage
  • payments.
  • Dowry violence refers to abuse, coercion or harassment connected with demands for
  • money, property or valuable goods associated with marriage.
  • Continuing demands: Harassment may occur when an agreed payment is considered
  • insufficient or when new demands arise after marriage.
  • Forms of violence:
  • • Physical: Beating, assault or other injury.
  • • Emotional and verbal: Insults, humiliation, threats and repeated criticism of the
  • woman or her family.
  • • Economic: Confiscating earnings, withholding necessities or pressuring her family to
  • transfer property.
  • • Coercive exclusion: Threatening abandonment or expelling her from the marital
  • home.
  • Social basis: Patriarchal entitlement and the treatment of marriage as a status transaction
  • can encourage the belief that the bride’s family owes continuing payments.
  • Consequences: Dowry harassment can produce injury, distress, debt, isolation and, in severe
  • cases, death.
  • Example: A woman is repeatedly threatened and assaulted because her parents refuse a
  • post-marriage demand for a car .
  • The Dowry Prohibition Act addresses marriage-connected dowry demands. Prevention also
  • requires social rejection of coercive payments and support for affected women.
  • indiacode.nic.in
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; forms and mechanisms — 3; consequences — 1;
  • example/prevention — 1.
  • 19(b). Analyse legal and policy protections in an educational institution’s response to
  • discrimination against a transgender student.
  • Discrimination against a transgender student should be treated as a violation of equal
  • participation and dignity, rather than as a problem with the student’s identity.
  • Legal foundation: Section 3 of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act prohibits
  • discrimination in educational establishments and their services. Section 13 requires
  • government-funded or recognised institutions to provide inclusive education and equal
  • opportunities in sports, recreation and leisure. indiacode.nic.in
  • Receive and address the complaint: The institution should provide an accessible reporting
  • process, document the complaint and investigate promptly and fairly.
  • Prevent further harm: It should stop bullying, exclusion and retaliation and provide
  • appropriate academic or counselling support.
  • Restore equal access: The student should have fair access to classes, examinations,
  • scholarships, facilities and extracurricular activities.
  • Respect identity and privacy: Institutional practice should use respectful communication,
  • protect confidential information and avoid unnecessary disclosure of the student’s
  • transgender status.
  • Review institutional policies: Anti-discrimination rules should explicitly address gender
  • identity. Staff training, inclusive teaching and consultation with transgender students can
  • help prevent recurrence.
  • Example: If a student is excluded from a college event because they are transgender, the
  • institution should restore participation, investigate the exclusion and correct the rule or
  • practice that enabled it.
  • Suggested marking: Legal foundation — 2; institutional response — 3; application — 1.
  • 20(a). Discuss patriarchy as an explanation of restrictions on women’s mobility.
  • Patriarchy is a system of social relations through which men, as a group, hold
  • disproportionate power and women face systematic disadvantage. It operates through
  • families, economic institutions, cultural norms and public life.
  • Control of sexuality: Restrictions on movement may regulate women’s friendships,
  • relationships and partner choices.
  • Family honour: Women’s behaviour is often linked to family reputation. Families may
  • impose curfews or require permission for travel while allowing men greater freedom.
  • Gendered division of labour: The expectation that women should remain responsible for
  • domestic work can limit participation in employment, education and public activities.
  • Economic dependence: Lack of income, transport or control over resources can make
  • women dependent on others for movement.
  • Violence and intimidation: Harassment in public spaces and abuse at home can discourage
  • independent movement.
  • Institutional reinforcement: Unequal hostel rules or restrictions on women’s travel can
  • reproduce patriarchal assumptions.
  • Example: Allowing a son to travel for higher education while requiring a daughter to remain
  • at home demonstrates unequal expectations based on gender.
  • Restrictions also vary by caste, class, age, disability and location. A patriarchal analysis shows
  • that mobility involves access to resources and decision-making power as well as physical
  • movement.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; mechanisms — 4; example/conclusion — 1.
  • 20(b). Explain how difference and plurality contribute to an inclusive gender programme.
  • Difference recognises that people have varied identities, circumstances and needs. Plurality
  • recognises that there are multiple gender identities, experiences and viewpoints rather than
  • one universal experience.
  • These ideas improve gender programmes in the following ways:
  • Avoiding a single model: A programme should not assume that all women—or all people of
  • any gender—face the same problems.
  • Recognising intersecting inequalities: Caste, class, disability, sexuality, religion, age and
  • location can shape access and participation.
  • Including diverse identities: Programmes should enable meaningful participation by
  • transgender, non-binary and other gender-diverse people.
  • Adapting support: Different barriers may require different responses, such as accessible
  • venues, childcare, local-language materials or transport assistance.
  • Sharing decision-making: Participants should help identify priorities, design activities and
  • evaluate outcomes.
  • Assessing unequal outcomes: Evaluation should examine who benefits and who remains
  • excluded, rather than relying only on total participation.
  • Example: An employment programme could combine skills training with childcare for
  • caregivers, accessibility support for disabled participants and measures against caste and
  • gender discrimination.
  • Difference and plurality therefore support substantive equality: people receive the
  • conditions needed to participate with dignity and agency.
  • Suggested marking: Concepts — 2; applications — 3; example/conclusion — 1.

questions.question: Give one example of an ecofeminist issue. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Give one example of an ecofeminist issue.
  • Deforestation and its effects on rural women is an ecofeminist issue. When forests
  • disappear, women responsible for collecting fuel, fodder and water may face increased work
  • and insecurity. Ecofeminism examines connections between environmental exploitation and
  • gender domination.

questions.question: What is work-life balance? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is work–life balance?
  • Work–life balance is the ability to manage paid work alongside personal life, family
  • responsibilities, care, leisure and rest without excessive conflict between these areas.

questions.question: Explain the measures that individuals can take to prevent cybercrime. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain measures individuals can take to prevent cybercrime.
  • Individuals can reduce cybercrime risks by:
  • • Using strong, unique passwords and multifactor authentication.
  • • Avoiding suspicious links and never sharing passwords or OTPs.
  • • Updating devices and reviewing privacy settings.
  • • Verifying requests before transferring money or disclosing personal information.
  • Marking: Any four appropriate measures — ½ mark each.

questions.question: Give one example of a changing gender norm. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Give one example of a changing gender norm.
  • Fathers sharing childcare and household work is an example. It challenges the belief that
  • caregiving and domestic responsibilities belong exclusively to women.

questions.question: What is a gender stereotype? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is a gender stereotype?
  • A gender stereotype is a generalised belief about the qualities, roles or behaviour expected
  • of people because of their gender.
  • Example: “Men are naturally better leaders than women.”

questions.question: What is reproductive labour? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• What is reproductive labour?
  • Reproductive labour is the work required to sustain people and reproduce everyday social
  • life, including cooking, cleaning, childcare and caring for elderly or ill people. It is often
  • unpaid and disproportionately performed by women, although it can also be paid.

questions.question: What is objectification? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is objectification?
  • Objectification means treating a person as an object for another person’s use or pleasure
  • while disregarding their agency, feelings and dignity.
  • Example: Valuing a woman only for her physical appearance rather than recognising her
  • abilities and choices.

questions.question: Explain the measures required to create a safe and gender-sensitive workplace. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain measures required for a safe and gender-sensitive workplace.
  • A safe and gender-sensitive workplace requires:
  • • Clear policies against discrimination and sexual harassment.
  • • Accessible complaint procedures, fair investigation and protection against retaliation.
  • • Gender-sensitisation programmes and respectful communication.
  • • Fair recruitment, equal opportunities and appropriate facilities.
  • Marking: Any four relevant measures — ½ mark each.

questions.question: Explain the measures that organisations can adopt to improve work–life balance / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• What measures can organisations adopt to improve work–life balance?
  • Organisations can provide flexible working arrangements, reasonable workloads, predictable
  • schedules, parental and caregiving leave, and childcare support. Respecting employees’ time
  • outside working hours also helps reduce work–family conflict.
  • Marking: Any four explained measures — ½ mark each.

questions.question: Name one agent of gender socialization. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Name one agent of gender socialisation.
  • Family. Through toys, clothing, household duties and expectations, families communicate
  • ideas about appropriate gender roles.
  • Other acceptable answers: schools, peer groups, media and religious institutions.

questions.question: Describe the major provisions of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe major provisions of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019.
  • Major provisions include:
  • • Prohibition of discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and access to
  • services.
  • • Inclusive education, welfare and healthcare measures.
  • • A framework for identity certification, grievance redress and a National Council for
  • Transgender Persons. indiacode.nic.in
  • Marking: Any two correctly explained provisions — 1 mark each.
  • Examiner’s note: The Act was amended in 2026. If assessing the original 2019 framework,
  • distinguish its original identity provisions from the amended law. dosje.gov.in

questions.question: Define sexual-orientation discrimination. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Define sexual-orientation discrimination.
  • Sexual-orientation discrimination means unfair treatment, exclusion or disadvantage
  • because of a person’s actual or perceived sexual orientation.
  • Example: Denying a qualified applicant employment because they are gay.

questions.question: Explain the legal and social measures for preventing dowry in India. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain legal and social measures for preventing dowry in India.
  • Legal measures: Enforce the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, which penalises demanding,
  • giving or taking dowry, subject to its statutory provisions and exceptions. indiacode.nic.in
  • Social measures: Promote dowry-free marriages, challenge demands disguised as gifts,
  • educate families and strengthen women’s economic independence.
  • Marking: Legal measures — 1; social measures — 1.

questions.question: Define domestic violence. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Define domestic violence.
  • Domestic violence refers to abusive acts, threats or controlling behaviour within domestic
  • relationships. It includes physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse; it is not
  • limited to physical assault. indiacode.gov.in

questions.question: Define intersectionality. / [CO1] [2x13 = 26]
questions.solution_html:
• Define intersectionality.
  • Intersectionality explains how gender interacts with caste, class, race, disability, sexuality
  • and other social relations to produce distinct experiences of privilege or disadvantage.
  • Example: A Dalit woman may face interconnected caste and gender discrimination that
  • cannot be understood by examining either separately.
